title: Executors, edges and supersteps
summary: A workflow is a directed graph: executors are the nodes, edges route typed messages between them. Execution proceeds in supersteps: all ready executors run in parallel, wait at a barrier, then the next messages are delivered.
useIf: You want explicit order, branching, fan-out and fan-in, with deterministic ordering and clean checkpoint boundaries.
avoidIf: The path is unknown in advance, or one agent loop can do the job without an explicit graph.

explain.md: **Executors** derive from `Executor` with handler methods (`@handler` in Python, `[MessageHandler]` on a `partial` class in C#) or are plain functions (`@executor`, `BindExecutor`). In Python `WorkflowContext[Sent, Yielded]` types what the handler sends downstream with `ctx.send_message()` and what it yields as workflow output with `ctx.yield_output()`; for example `WorkflowContext[Never, str]` is an output-only handler. Do not mix annotations with explicit `@handler(input=..., output=..., workflow_output=...)` parameters [[tr15]]. Agents join the graph through `AgentExecutor` or directly as nodes.

**Supersteps** follow a modified Pregel (bulk synchronous parallel) model. Each superstep collects pending messages, routes them over edges, runs all target executors concurrently, waits at a barrier, then queues new messages. That gives a deterministic order and a checkpoint boundary after every step. Consequence: if a fan-out has one branch that is a chain and another that is one slow executor, the chain stalls at the barrier; merge steps into one executor for truly independent paths [[tr14]]. **Builders are mutable, built workflows are immutable**, and executor or agent instances shared across workflows share mutable state, so build fresh instances per workflow [[tr14]].

explain.title: One superstep
explain.alt: Pending messages are routed over edges, target executors run concurrently, a barrier waits for all, then new messages and a checkpoint are produced for the next superstep.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  P[Pending messages] --> R[Route over edges]
  R --> E1[Executor A]
  R --> E2[Executor B]
  E1 --> B[Barrier]
  E2 --> B
  B --> C[Checkpoint and new messages]
  C --> P

blocks.code:
class Upper(Executor):
    @handler
    async def to_upper(self, text: str, ctx: WorkflowContext[str]) -> None:
        await ctx.send_message(text.upper())

workflow = (
    WorkflowBuilder(start_executor=detector, output_from=[finalize])
    .add_edge(detector, assistant, condition=lambda m: not is_spam(m))
    .add_edge(detector, spam_handler, condition=lambda m: is_spam(m))
    .add_edge(assistant, finalize)
    .build()
)
async for event in workflow.run(input_message, stream=True):
    if event.type == 'output':
        print(event.data)
events = await workflow.run(input_message)      # non-streaming
print(events.get_outputs())

explain.title: A throwing edge condition fails the run
explain.md: In a switch-case group the default target runs only when every predicate returns false. If a predicate raises, the workflow fails and the message is not routed to the default. Catch parse errors in the condition and fail closed (return false) [[tr16]].

whereToUse: Pipelines with branches: classify, route, handle, finalize
Parallel analysis with aggregation (fan-out then fan-in)
Mixed deterministic and model nodes, such as rules as functions and judgment as agents
Anything that must be checkpointed per step and resumed

use: You can name the steps and the conditions between them
Several branches should run in parallel with a defined merge
Auditors want a trace of which executor ran in which superstep
avoid: Open-ended tasks where the model should choose the path
Tiny scripts where an ordinary function call chain is clearer
Independent branches of unequal length inside one fan-out: the barrier makes the short path wait
flips: A branch is a long chain beside a short one: merge the chain into one executor or split into separate workflows
You need output from early steps for a UI: designate them with `intermediate_output_from` instead of final output

pitfalls.symptom: A fast branch waits for a slow one
pitfalls.cause: The superstep barrier waits for every executor in the step
pitfalls.fix: Merge chained steps into one executor, or restructure the graph

pitfalls.symptom: Python 1.0 samples break: executors are referenced by string names
pitfalls.cause: Since 1.0.0b260210 builder methods take instances, not string names
pitfalls.fix: Pass executor instances to `add_edge` and friends

pitfalls.symptom: Two workflows share mutable state unexpectedly
pitfalls.cause: Executor or agent instances were reused across workflows
pitfalls.fix: Build fresh executor and agent instances per workflow

scenarios.title: Triage with parallel enrichment
scenarios.situation: Incoming claims are classified, then three enrichment calls (policy lookup, fraud score, document summary) run, then an adjuster agent decides. Fraud score takes 8 seconds; the others 1 to 2.
unknowns: Can the summary start before classification ends?
scenarios.question: How do you model the enrichment?

options.name: Fan-out edge to the three enrichers, fan-in barrier edge to the adjuster
options.why: They run concurrently in one superstep, so the step costs the slowest call (about 8 seconds), not the sum (about 11).
options.tradeoff: The adjuster waits for the slowest, and a failure needs explicit handling.

options.name: Chain the three enrichers with direct edges
options.why: Sequential supersteps add latency: about 11 seconds before the adjuster even starts.
options.tradeoff: Right when each step depends on the previous one's output.

options.name: One executor that calls all three with `asyncio.gather`
options.tradeoff: You lose per-step events, checkpoints and observability for each enrichment.

flips.if: Fraud score is optional and slow
flips.then: Make it a separate branch that finishes later, or time-box it inside its executor.

flips.if: Each enrichment needs its own retry policy

scenarios.takeaway: Fan-out costs the slowest branch; chains cost the sum.

scenarios.title: Routing on a model's classification
scenarios.situation: An agent returns JSON saying Spam, NotSpam or Uncertain. Malformed JSON sometimes occurs. Each outcome goes to a different handler.
unknowns: How often is the JSON malformed?
scenarios.question: How do you route?

options.name: A switch-case group with explicit cases and a default to the human-review handler, with conditions that fail closed on parse errors
options.why: Default catches Uncertain and any case where all predicates are false, and parse errors return false instead of raising.
options.tradeoff: More code per condition; remember a raising predicate fails the run.

options.name: Two conditional edges for Spam and NotSpam only
options.why: Uncertain output has no edge and the message goes nowhere.
options.tradeoff: Fine for a strictly binary classifier with validated output.

options.name: Let each handler decide whether to act
options.tradeoff: Routing logic scatters and is hard to audit.

flips.if: The classifier uses structured output with a schema
flips.then: Parse errors become rare and simple conditions suffice.

flips.if: More than one handler may apply

scenarios.takeaway: Design the default path first; unknown outputs need somewhere safe to go.

quiz.q: A fan-out sends work to three executors taking 1.5, 2 and 8 seconds, then a fan-in aggregator takes 1 second. In one run with a superstep barrier, what is the minimum time to the aggregator's completion, in seconds?
quiz.explain: The superstep waits for the slowest executor (8 s), then the next superstep runs the aggregator (1 s): 9 s. A sequential chain would take 11.5 + 1 = 12.5 s.

quiz.q: Which statement about supersteps is correct?
options: Executors in a superstep run one at a time in insertion order
Checkpoints are written only when the workflow ends
Edges are evaluated lazily during executor runs
All ready executors run concurrently and wait at a barrier before messages for the next superstep are delivered
quiz.explain: The modified Pregel model runs targets concurrently, then a barrier, then new messages. Checkpoints are created at the end of each superstep.

flashcards.back: The types an executor sends downstream (`send_message`) and yields as workflow output (`yield_output`); `Never` marks no downstream messages.
Direct, conditional, switch-case, multi-selection (fan-out) and fan-in.

flashcards.front: Why can a fast branch be slow?
flashcards.back: Supersteps have a barrier, so a fan-out step finishes only when the slowest executor finishes.
